title: forty days
hook: forty days; giving something up is a way of paying attention

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Our Father, and the family word at the start of it. Your line was: not a stranger. Who did you treat like family? Day fifteen.

One Wednesday a year, something strange happens at work. The woman at the next desk has a smudge of black on her forehead. Then the guy at the coffee shop. Then a kid on the train. Someone reaches over to tell them they've got dirt on their face, and they smile and say: it's Ash Wednesday. For the rest of the season, a Catholic friend might be off chocolate, or off social media, or eating fish on Fridays. From the outside it can look like a diet. It isn't about the chocolate at all. Today, forty days of paying attention.
screen: `A SMUDGE ON THE FOREHEAD.` → `IT'S ASH WEDNESDAY.` → `IT ISN'T ABOUT THE CHOCOLATE.`

segments.voice: Lent is the season of forty days before Easter. The English word is old: it comes from an Old English word for spring, when the days lengthen. And forty comes up again and again in the Bible, often around a time of testing. Noah's rain falls forty days. Moses stays on the mountain forty days. Israel wanders forty years. And in Matthew's Gospel, right after his baptism, Jesus goes into the desert, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "And when he had fasted forty days and forty nights, afterwards he was hungry." Lent is Catholics walking alongside those forty days. It starts with the ashes. The priest or minister marks a cross on the forehead with ash, and may say words from Genesis: "dust thou art, and into dust thou shalt return." It sounds grim. Catholics hear it as honest. You won't be here forever, so what are you doing with the time? Then come the three old practices, the same three Jesus names in the Sermon on the Mount: prayer, fasting, and giving to the poor. Catholics are asked to fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, and to skip meat on the Fridays of Lent. Some give something up for the whole season. Here's the idea underneath. Give up something small, and every reach for it becomes a moment of noticing. The reach becomes a reminder. The empty space where the chocolate used to be becomes a little room for prayer, or for someone else. Less, on purpose. Some Catholics also add something: a daily walk, a visit to someone lonely, money set aside for the hungry. And the forty days only make sense because of where they end: Easter morning.
screen: `LENT — THE DAYS LENGTHEN.` · `FORTY: NOAH, MOSES, THE DESERT.` · `DUST THOU ART.` · `PRAYER, FASTING, GIVING.` · then, large: `THE REACH BECOMES A REMINDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. A seventy-five-second sit. Think of one small thing you reach for without thinking. Your phone. A snack. A complaint. Don't give it up yet. Just picture yourself reaching for it, and stopping, hand in the air. What would you notice in that moment instead? Stay there, breathing slowly, in the pause before the reach. If you pray, you can offer that pause to God. The bell holds the time.
Lent. Forty days before Easter, of prayer, fasting and giving, where less becomes a way of paying attention. Fifteenth word.
Your line: less, on purpose. Today, skip one small thing you'd usually reach for, and each time you miss it, let it remind you of someone. Day fifteen.

howItsDone: Catholics receive ashes on Ash Wednesday, fast on Ash Wednesday and Good Friday, abstain from meat on Fridays in Lent, and take on prayer, fasting and almsgiving for the forty days before Easter.
